_comment: Everything the wall reader is allowed to differ on, in one file. Nothing here is a fact about buildings - those live in the code. These are the numbers an office may legitimately set differently, and every one of them is a measurement in millimetres or in PDF points, never a coordinate taken from any particular drawing. This file is merged over the 'walls' section of plan_reading.json, so a setting given here wins and anything left out keeps its existing value.
_reader_note: Which reader measures the walls. 'cvdetect' is the computer-vision reader: it closes the drawing into solid bands, measures each band's thickness with a distance transform and reduces it to a centreline by skeletonisation, so A WALL IS REPORTED ONCE rather than once per pair of drawn faces - an external wall drawn with a lining and a hatch boundary gave three overlapping candidates before. 'legacy' is the face-pairing reader in pipeline/plan/walls.py, kept and switchable so the two can be compared on the same plan and so a deployed server can be changed back without a rebuild. Both hand back the same canonical record and both go through the same junction, free-tail, detached-structure, outer/inner and description pass, so nothing downstream - the overlay, the model, the CSVs, the opening evidence - depends on which one ran.
_thickness_note: A wall is two parallel faces this far apart. Below the minimum it is a lining, a hatch boundary or a piece of joinery; above the maximum it is two separate walls with a room between them, or a boundary line paired with an eave.
_length_note: Anything shorter than the floor is furniture, hatching, a door swing or a fragment - never a wall. Measured: at 200 mm a dining chair (440 mm across, with its back drawn 76 mm behind it) is a wall, and so is every tile corner and every 6-point square on the sheet; at 600 mm they are not, and the walls a house is actually built from are all still there. Between the floor and the connected minimum a candidate is only kept when it meets another wall: a short stretch joined to the building is a pier, a return or a partition stub, while a short stretch joined to nothing is a bench top.
_tolerance_note: Two drawn pieces are the same face when they sit within this many points of the same line. A point is 1/72 inch, so it is a tolerance on the paper and means the same at any drawing scale. It must stay well under the thinnest wall the office builds, because a wall IS two lines a thickness apart: at 1:100 a tolerance of 3 points is 106 mm, which is wider than a 90 mm wall, so a wall's own two faces merge into one line and the wall disappears. Measured on one floor plan, going from 0.6 to 3 points took the walls at a thickness the office builds from 38 of 40 down to 21 of 27. The junction tolerance below is a different quantity and is deliberately much larger - it allows for an unclosed corner, not for a wall.
_overlap_note: Two parallel faces are one wall only when they run together for this share of the shorter of them. A face that shares a tenth of its length with another is passing it, not facing it.
_dimension_line_note: A dimension line is drawn thinner than a wall face, and where the PDF states a stroke width that is the cheapest way to tell them apart. Measured on the plan sets in use, an absolute threshold in points is the wrong instrument and it was turned off because of what it cost: offices draw wall lines at 0.25 and 0.35 pt, and a wall face recovered from a page read as a picture is one pixel wide, which is 0.36 pt at the resolution used - so a threshold of 0.5 pt threw away real walls on every plan set tried (one floor plan lost 30 of its 90 walls and 133 m of wall). Zero switches it off. Set it only after checking the weights the office actually plots walls at, and check the wall count before and after.
_hatching_note: Hatching is many parallel strokes a short distance apart, repeated across an area. A band of faces packed closer together than this, and more of them in the band than the number below, is hatching and is dropped before pairing. The count has to be generous, and this is why: measured at building scale, the gap between hatch strokes and the gap between a wall's skin, cavity, frame and lining are the same size, so separation alone cannot tell them apart - only how many there are in one place can. A band limit of 4 read a brick-veneer external wall as hatching and cost 48 m of real wall on one floor plan and 28 m on another. At 12 the guard is armed and touches nothing on any plan set tried, which is what a guard should do.
_junction_note: Walls meet at corners (L), at partitions running into them (T) and at crossings (+). Two walls are joined when each one's thickness band reaches the other's run, within the tolerance above. The result is a graph - walls are the nodes, junctions the edges - which is what later stages use to close rooms and to tell the outside of the building from the inside.
_outer_inner_note: An outer wall is one with nothing but open paper on one side of it: a ray cast out from it crosses no other wall before it leaves the building. That test is geometry, so it holds on an L-shaped or a U-shaped plan, where a rectangle around the building would not. A wall the ray test cannot decide is reported as unknown rather than guessed.
_lettering_note: Letters are not walls. A sheet stored as a picture has its lines recovered by looking for continuous runs of dark pixels, and a word set in capitals is one - so every room name became a wall lying across its own room. A line counts as lettering when this share of it runs inside the box of one printed line of text. Containment, not overlap: a real wall passing under a room label is many times longer than the label, so only a fraction of it is inside and it is kept.
_group_note: A building is a connected group of walls: they reach each other, corner to corner and partition to wall, all the way round. Touching one other line is not that - the two lines of a legend row touch each other, so do the sides of a car drawn in a garage and the witness lines beside a dimension figure, and every one of those was appearing on the marked-up sheet as a wall. A group smaller than this encloses nothing, so it is not part of the building. Four, because a closed shape takes four walls. Such candidates are still listed with the reason; they are kept off the marked-up sheet and out of the model, where a line that is not a wall does real harm.
_inside_the_plan_note: A building is drawn between its dimension strings, never through them. The strings printed outside the room names bound the part of the sheet the plan is on, and a pair of parallel lines outside that is a dimension string's own witness lines. Those are the worst false wall there is: a 90 mm dimension has its two witness lines exactly 90 mm apart, which passes every thickness test, and they are drawn on the same line as the wall face they measure to, so they merge with it. Turn this off only on a sheet that prints no dimension strings outside its plan; where there is nothing to work from it already removes nothing.
_slenderness_note: A wall is longer than it is thick. Two lines 230 mm apart that run together for 230 mm are a square, and a square is a column, a symbol, a hatch cell or a fragment - never a wall. Worth having alongside the length floor because it holds at any scale and on any size of building: the floor is a size and can be wrong for a small one, but nothing as wide as it is long is a wall.
_free_tail_note: A wall ends where it meets another wall, or at the outside of the building. It never ends in the middle of empty paper out in the margin. The stretch beyond a wall's outermost junction is cut off, but only where that stretch is outside the area the room names are printed in - inside the building a wall genuinely can stop free, at a doorway, at the end of a nib or at a return, and that is the distinction that makes this safe. A tail shorter than the figure below is left alone as ordinary drafting.
_symbol_note: A plan does not only break its walls where an opening goes - it draws the opening. A window is drawn inside the wall's own thickness: the wall's two faces carry on past it and between them the glass, the frame and the sashes are drawn. How many lines are drawn in there says which window it is, and that is a drafting convention rather than a number to tune: three or more are the overlapping sashes of a sliding window, two are a fixed pane and its frame, one is a highlight or an obscure panel. A wall is solid, so nothing is drawn inside a wall.
_swing_note: A hinged door is drawn as its swing, and the arc's radius is the door leaf - so a plan set carries its door widths in its geometry whether or not it prints a schedule. A swing is recognised by shape, never by a particular size: a path containing a curve whose box is about as wide as it is tall. A curved path much wider than it is tall is a leader, a cloud or a piece of lettering.
_small_mark_note: The arrows on a sliding sash and the cross on a fixed panel. Supporting evidence only: a short stroke is a hundred other things on a plan, and what makes one an arrow is that it is found inside an opening.
_evidence_note: Two readings are of the same opening when they claim the same stretch of wall, or when they sit on the same wall nearer than this to each other. A door's swing is drawn from the hinge and a break is measured between the jambs, so the two can sit alongside rather than on top - and nearer than a door is wide, on one wall, there is not room for two openings.
_second_look_note: A face that found no partner is tried again with the thickness range widened by this much. The range is what stops a wall being paired with the wrong line, so it is deliberately tight - and a wall drawn a little outside it, a rendered skin or one with a service duct in it, then loses its partner and disappears. Widening only for the faces that failed keeps the tight range where it is working.
_lone_face_note: A wall drawn with one of its faces missing is still a wall: the other face is behind a cupboard, drawn as joinery, broken into pieces too short to merge, or not drawn at all where the plan cuts a bulkhead. Such a face can be kept as a wall with the nearest thickness the office builds ASSUMED, said out loud on the record, on screen and in the spreadsheet. It is OFF here because of what it measured: even required to run between two other walls, it added 66 walls to a floor plan that has about 40, and the marked-up sheet showed them lying over the kitchen joinery, the cars in the garage, the bathroom fittings and the tile pattern. On this evidence a lone line cannot be told from joinery on these drawings. Turn it on only where the office draws walls with one face and check the marked-up sheet before trusting the result.
_junction_break_note: A break where another wall runs in is a junction, not a door - both stop the wall's two faces at the same place and they mean opposite things. A junction break is about as wide as the wall that made it: a 90 mm partition breaks a wall for 90 mm, while a door breaks it for 820 mm, and a partition arriving at one jamb of that door does not make the door a junction. This is the share of the break the wall running in has to account for.
_outline_note: Everything belonging to a building is joined to the rest of it, so the largest group of walls that reach each other is the building and its extent bounds it - nothing outside is a wall of this building, not the eave line, not the block boundary, not the roof extent drawn round it. Two guards, both measured: the group has to hold a clear share of the sheet's walls, and its box has to look like a building. On a sheet drawn as a picture the biggest connected piece was twenty walls lying along one side of the house, a band 350 by 90 points on a drawing 770 across, and half the real walls were reported as outside the building.
_detached_note: A carport, a pergola, a shed and a detached garage are drawn on the same sheet and are not the same building. They are not joined to it - that is what detached means - so the house forms one connected group of walls and each outbuilding forms its own, which is what the junctions already say. The largest group is the building; every other group large enough to enclose something is a detached structure, kept in the table, drawn in its own colour and left out of the building's model. Nothing is judged unless the largest group really is a building.
_dash_note: A dashed line is not always stored as one. Every plan set here exports its dashes as many short separate segments with a solid dash pattern, so the PDF's own property says nothing - on one floor plan all 5,595 paths are marked solid, including the roof extent that is plainly dashed on the page. What is left is the shape of the line: a run drawn in this many short pieces separated by gaps no longer than this is a dashed line, whatever the file calls it.
_geometry_only_note: Nothing here decides what is a wall from a word printed on the sheet. A word is an office's habit - one writes EXTENT OF ROOF, another ROOF LINE OVER, a third nothing at all - while a dashed line is a dashed line on every drawing ever plotted, an arrowhead points at something on every one of them, and a panel of printed matter sits against an edge on every one of them.
_panel_note: A title block, a legend, an abbreviations list and a block of notes are the same thing to this reader: a dense rectangle of text, ruled into rows, pushed against an edge of the sheet so it stays clear of the drawing - and those rules are parallel lines a few millimetres apart at drawing scale, which is to say they are walls to anything that looks only at the lines. The sheet is divided into squares a fraction of its own size, so the same settings work on an A4 and an A0.
_leader_note: A note's leader finishes in an arrowhead, and a wall never points at anything - so an arrowhead at the end of a line should say it is a leader. It is OFF here because of what it measured: a wall's end is precisely where the arrowheads of the dimensions that measure it are drawn, so the rule set aside the building's longest and most obviously real walls - 34 of one floor plan's 88, including its 19.6 m external wall, and 31 of another's 71. Requiring the arrowhead to sit on the line and past its end rather than merely near it changed nothing, because a dimension's arrowhead sits against the very wall face it measures to. Turn it on only where an office draws its leaders differently, and check the wall count.
_raster_swing_note: A plan set can be published as pictures: one of the sets in use draws its whole plan as embedded images, so the quarter circle every hinged door is drawn with is pixels rather than a curve. The page is then rendered and each outline on it is tested for being an arc of a circle - it must lie on one, turn through about a quarter, and have the radius of a door leaf in millimetres through the sheet's own scale. Hough circles were not used: they answer 'is there a full circle here', which returns every fixture and every letter O, and a door swing is precisely the case where most of the circle is absent.
_raster_swing_when_note: When to look. The count of curve paths in the PDF is the cheap test and it is kept, but it is not enough on its own: the picture-drawn set has 12 to 24 curve paths on every sheet - its border, its north point, its clouded revisions - so a count alone would never look at the very file that needs it. What decides is the outcome, as it does for the wall lines: the page is read as a picture when the sheet's own geometry put no door swing on any of its walls.
_line_source_note: A sheet's own vector geometry is always read first - it is the drawing's exact line work, and nothing recovered from pixels can beat it. The page is only read as a picture when that geometry did not trace a building, and a building is a closed shape, so it takes at least this many walls. The test is the outcome, never a count of how much geometry the page held: an earlier version switched whenever a sheet had fewer than 200 drawn lines, and re-read sheets whose sparse vector geometry was perfectly good. The fuller of the two readings still wins, so exact line work is never displaced by pixels that found less.
_raster_lines_note: Reading the lines off a sheet whose drawing is stored as a picture. Every value here is a measurement in millimetres, in degrees or in dots per inch - never a coordinate, a count or a name from any particular drawing. The detector itself is OpenCV's Line Segment Detector, which needs no parameters at all: it grows each line from the image's own gradients and validates it against how often such a region would arise by chance, so it carries no length, no threshold and no kernel to be set per drawing. What is configured here is only what to do with the segments it returns.

raster_lines._render_dpi_note: How finely the page is rendered before its lines are read. At 1:100 a 90 mm wall is about 7 pixels wide at 200 DPI, which is enough to measure its two faces apart; rendering finer costs time and memory on a large sheet without finding more wall faces. A sheet drawn at a smaller scale, or an office that plots very fine, may want more.
raster_lines._straightness_note: How far from horizontal or vertical a segment may lie and still be taken as a wall face. A plan is drawn on the axes, so anything at an angle is a door swing, a roof diagonal, a stair nosing, a hatch stroke, a note's leader or a piece of lettering - and a wall is found by pairing two faces that run parallel, so an off-axis segment cannot be one. This allowance is for a scanned sheet's own skew and the sub-pixel jitter of an edge detector; it is not a licence to accept a diagonal.
raster_lines._min_segment_note: The shortest run worth calling a piece of a wall face, in millimetres of building. At drawing scale a stroke shorter than this is a letter, a dimension tick, an arrowhead barb, a hatch stroke, or the fragment the detector returns where one line crosses another. It is a floor on the tracing and not on a wall: the pieces that remain are joined into one face afterwards, across gaps as wide as an opening, so a real face broken into short pieces is still recovered. Setting it far higher starves that joining step of the pieces it joins.
raster_lines._max_line_width_note: A run wider than the thickest wall the office builds is not a line at all: it is a filled area, a solid poche, a band of shading, or a photographic edge in a scan. Pairing it with anything beside it would report the fill itself as a wall. Keep this in step with max_wall_thickness_mm above.
raster_lines._prejoin_note: A Line Segment Detector does not return an edge; it returns the pieces of one. On a sheet stored as a picture a wall face that the plan draws as one line comes back broken wherever the ink thins, wherever another line crosses it and wherever the image was compressed - each piece sitting a fraction of a point off its neighbours, because an edge grown from gradients is placed to sub-pixel precision and the pixels disagree. Measured on one floor plan, a single 2.9 m internal wall arrived as nine segments spread over half a point. That jitter is smaller than the face merging downstream can see - it buckets by collinear_tolerance_points, which is deliberately held well under the thinnest wall the office builds and so can never be widened to cover it - so the pieces became two or three separate faces a few tens of millimetres apart and then competed with each other for the far face of the same wall, each pairing taking only the stretch it covered. Thirty real internal walls on that one sheet were lost this way, and none of them could carry a reason, because a wall that was never formed is not in the reading at all. The gap is how far apart two pieces of one edge may sit along the run - they have to be consecutive within it, from either side, because the detector's pieces overlap by a fraction of a point as often as they leave a gap, and a piece starting well back inside a run is a second line lying alongside rather than a continuation. The offset is how far one piece may sit off the line of the other, and it has a window it must sit inside: measured on these renders the pieces of one edge are spread by up to 1.6 points, while the thinnest wall an office builds is 1.98 points at 1:100 - so below 1.6 the pieces are not rejoined and real walls are lost, and at 1.98 a wall's own two faces would be averaged into one line and the wall would disappear. 1.8 is the middle of that window. It is capped at the thinnest wall in code whatever is set here. This repairs THIS reader's output and is never applied to the sheet's own vector geometry, which states each line once, exactly, and has no jitter to repair.
raster_lines._stroke_edge_note: A Line Segment Detector finds edges, not lines - it reports where the image changes from light to dark along a straight front, and a plotted line has two such fronts, one down each side of the stroke. So every drawn wall face arrives as two segments a stroke's width apart, and left alone each of them pairs with the far face of the wall separately: one wall is then reported two, three or four times over, each copy with a thickness a stroke's width out. Two segments are the two sides of one stroke when they run together and sit closer than the stroke the detector itself measured for them - which is self-tuning in the same way the detector is, a heavily plotted sheet and a finely plotted one each supplying their own figure, and which stays far below a real wall: at 1:100 a 90 mm wall's two faces are 7 pixels apart at 200 DPI while the two sides of the line drawing one of them are 2 to 3. Turn this off only to see the raw edges.

_reader_status: TEMPORARY - set to 'cvdetect' for evaluation on the web interface, NOT because it measured better. It does not: on the third plan set it reads 1 opening against the face-pairing reader's 15, and a 23-sheet set takes 35s against 21s. What it does read well is the picture-published set, where it now gets 9 openings against 11 and its breaks match exactly (29 against 29). Set this back to 'legacy' when the evaluation is done - the file is re-read while the server is running, so neither direction needs a restart.
